Use the genitive for possession: der Name des Mannes, das Haus der Familie.
Form the genitive: des / eines + -s / -es for masculine and neuter, der / einer for feminine and plural.
Use “-s” with proper names: Maras Vater, Ludwigs Lampe.
Use “von + dative” as an alternative in spoken German.
Use the prepositions that take the genitive: wegen, trotz, während, statt.

It's May. Mara's parents are in Berlin for the first time. Ludwig has prepared a surprise for Mara's father: he's taken him onto the roof of a block of flats in Prenzlauer Berg, where a neighbour keeps beehives. Mara translates.
Right, here we are. This is the roof terrace of the house next door. And these are the bees of my friend Klaus.
Dad, these are the bees of Ludwig's friend. The one he plays chess with. He's an urban beekeeper.
Bees on the roof? In the middle of the city? What do they live on?
On lime trees. Berlin is the city of lime trees. When the limes are in blossom, in June, the whole city smells of honey.
And despite the traffic and the exhaust fumes, the honey is good?
Very good, actually. Because of the many parks and gardens, the bees have more flowers here than in the countryside. At least that's what Klaus says.
Dad, you should taste Klaus's honey. Instead of coffee this afternoon.
Tell him I'd like to give him a jar of my acacia honey. In exchange.
An exchange! That's the spirit of the old East. Klaus will be delighted.
Mara, please ask him whose idea it was. To bring me here.
Mine. Your daughter has told me so much about your bees. I thought the father of such a good nurse must be a good beekeeper.

The genitive adds “-s” or “-es”: des Mannes (“MAH-nes”), des Hauses (“HOW-zes”), meines Vaters (“FAH-ters”).
“VES-sen”: the e is short, ss = s.
“Linde” with a short i; “Unter den Linden” is Berlin's famous boulevard.
The genitive expresses possession, like English “of” or “'s”. In German, the “owner” comes AFTER the thing owned (as in “the house of my parents”):

In the masculine and neuter, the noun takes “-s” (longer words: des Vaters, des Lehrers) or “-es” (short one-syllable words: des Mannes, des Kindes, des Hauses). Feminine and plural nouns take nothing.
“n”-type masculine nouns (chapter 33) take “-n”, not “-s”: des Kollegen, des Studenten, des Herrn.
An adjective in the genitive almost always takes “-en”: des alten Mannes, der jungen Frau, meines besten Freundes.

With names, you just add “-s”, without an apostrophe (unlike English), and the name comes FIRST: Maras Vater, Ludwigs Lampe, Lenas Bäckerei. Names ending in -s, -ß, -z take an apostrophe: Klaus’ Bienen.
In everyday speech, the genitive is often replaced by “von + dative”:
The question “Wessen…?” = Whose…? is fairly formal. In speech people often say: “Von wem ist das?” or “Wem gehört das?”.
Wegen des Regens bleiben wir zu Hause.
Trotz des Wetters gehen wir spazieren.
Während des Besuchs hat es nur einmal geregnet.
Statt des Kaffees trinken wir Tee.
In spoken German, many Germans use the dative after “wegen” and “trotz”: “wegen dem Regen”. In writing and in exams, use the genitive.
Compare: “weil es regnet” (clause with a verb) = “wegen des Regens” (just a noun). “obwohl es regnet” = “trotz des Regens”.
The Brandt family's bakery is old.
Spoken, instead of “das Auto meines Bruders”:
My father's bees are in Sibiu.
Because of the traffic I was late.

The visit of Mara's parents lasted ten days. It was the first time they had left Romania. Her mother had packed three suitcases, two of them full of food: zacuscă (a roasted vegetable spread), sausages, cheese from Rășinari, a jar of pickled peppers and, of course, six jars of honey. At BER airport, a customs officer asked whose suitcases they were. Mara's father pointed at his wife. The customs officer opened the first suitcase, sniffed the sausage and let them through with a smile.

The parents stayed in Mara's flat. Mara slept on the sofa, where Andrei had already slept, and Fritz slept in front of the door, because he had immediately declared Mara's mother his favourite person. The reason was simple: she secretly slipped him sausage under the table, despite Mara's protests and despite Ludwig's strict diet for the dog.

On the second day, Mara's mother got to know Lena better. They had met in August in Sibiu, but back then Lena had only been “Mara's friend from Berlin”. Now she was her son's girlfriend. At five in the morning Mara's mother was standing in the bakery, in Lena's apron, watching Lena bake bread. She didn't speak German, Lena didn't speak Romanian. Even so, they talked for two hours, with their hands, with flour, with photos on the phone and with the name “Andrei”, which came up roughly every minute.
Mara, tell her she's too thin. And tell her that when Andrei was little, he always forgot his socks under the bed. She needs to know what she's getting into.
Tell her I already know that. He's left three pairs of socks at my place. In a single week.

The two women laughed so loudly that Emre came out of the storeroom to see what was going on. From that moment on, Mara's mother called Lena only “my girl”, and Lena learnt her first Romanian words: “mulțumesc” (thank you), “pâine” (bread) and “Andrei e un dezastru” (Andrei is a disaster).

On the evening of the third day, Mrs Hoffmann invited everyone up to the fourth floor. Mara's mother brought a jar of zacuscă, and Mrs Hoffmann, who otherwise ate almost nothing, ate three slices of bread with it. Then she sat down at the piano and asked Mara about a Romanian song her parents knew. Mara hummed the tune of “Ciocârlia” (“The Lark”), an old folk song about a lark. Mrs Hoffmann listened twice, then played it, first slowly, then faster and faster and wilder, with the fingers of a woman who was not ninety-one but nineteen. Mara's mother cried. Mara's father sat motionless, his big hands on his knees, and when the song ended, he stood up and kissed the old pianist's hand. The way it used to be done in his village. Mrs Hoffmann blushed like a young girl.

With her father it was different. He was a quiet man who felt lost in the big city. The underground seemed too noisy to him, the streets too wide, the people too hurried. On the third day he stood for hours at the window of Mara's flat and looked at the chestnut tree in the courtyard. Mara was worried. Because of the language, because of the city, because of the distance from his bees.

Ludwig saw it too. Ludwig always saw everything. On the fourth day he knocked on Mara's door, with his hat on and a cheeky smile. “Tell your father to put on old clothes,” he said. “And tell him he mustn't be afraid of heights.”

Klaus, Ludwig's chess friend, lived two houses further along, on the fifth floor of an old building without a lift. On the roof he had built a small terrace, with tomatoes in pots, two deckchairs and four colourful beehives. From there you could see over the roofs of Prenzlauer Berg as far as the TV tower. The bees flew back and forth in the morning sun, like golden sparks.

Mara's father stopped in the doorway to the terrace. Then he walked slowly to the hives, without a veil, without gloves, and laid his hand on the wood of one of the boxes. Klaus wanted to warn him, but Ludwig held him back by the arm. The bees settled on Mara's father's hand, on his arm, on his shoulder. Not one of them stung him.
That's impossible. They sting me every week. How does he do that?
He says you have to breathe calmly. Bees sense a person's fear. He hasn't been afraid of them for forty years.

The two beekeepers, the Berliner and the Romanian, spent the whole morning on the roof. Klaus showed the frames of his hives, Mara's father showed how to recognise a queen. They didn't share a language, but that didn't matter. Mara translated at first, then less and less, and in the end not at all. She sat with Ludwig in one of the deckchairs, drank tea from a flask and watched her father, who was smiling for the first time in days.
You see, Mara? A person doesn't need a language, but something they love. Then they find friends everywhere.

On the last day of the visit, at the airport, Mara's father hugged Ludwig goodbye. He said something in Romanian, quietly, and Mara had to translate, even though her voice was shaking: “He says: thank you for looking after my daughter. He says a man who understands bees also understands people.” Ludwig nodded and shook his hand. Then he gave him a small jar. On the label, in Ludwig's big, shaky handwriting, it said: “Lime-blossom honey. The roof at Kastanienallee 35. From Klaus and Ludwig. For the bees in Sibiu.”
On the plane, her mother told her later on the phone, her father held the little jar in both hands for the whole two hours. He didn't want to put it in the suitcase. “It's too precious,” he had said.
